item.title: Number of non-EU dentists in NL doubles in five years
item.description:
Number of non-EU dentists in NL doubles in five years

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of dentists trained outside the EU who are moving to the Netherlands to help fill a chronic national shortage has more than doubled in five years, with recent arrivals coming from countries including Syria, South Africa, Turkey, Brazil and Iraq.

One in four dentists now working in the country qualified abroad, according to the dentists’ association KNMT, and in Zeeland more than half were trained overseas.

Figures from the Amsterdam dental school ACTA, which runs the admissions process for applicants from outside the EU, show 120 people are sitting its professional competence test this year, compared with 53 in 2021, the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported.

In total, 2,287 dentists with a foreign diploma are working in the Netherlands, a number rising by 150 to 200 a year.

Lack of national funding 
The reliance on overseas recruits is partly due to a lack of education funding for Dutch students. Thousands apply but places are very limited. Etienne Verheijck, education director for the ACTA, called that “a policy choice by the education ministry.”

KNMT chair Hans de Vries called it “painful” that motivated young people are rejected by a lottery system, sometimes three times in a row, while the gap is filled from abroad.

The shortage is expected to grow, and the government’s own capacity advisory body has for years urged ministers to open more training places.

Checking your dentist is registered
To work in the Netherlands, dentists with a non-EU diploma must pass a competence test and learn Dutch before they can join the official BIG register of healthcare professionals. Those with an EU diploma need only meet the language requirement.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said it regularly receives reports of people performing treatments such as root canals without being registered. De Vries said dentists may work under a registered colleague’s supervision while they qualify, but treating patients unsupervised is improper and potentially unlawful.

Patients can check whether their own dentist appears on the BIG register, which is public and free to search. Dental care in the Netherlands works differently from many other countries, and full practices unable to take on new patients are already a common complaint.

item.title: Dutch boy, 12, seriously injured in fall in Austrian alps
item.description:
Dutch boy, 12, seriously injured in fall in Austrian alps

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 12-year-old Dutch boy is being treated in intensive care after falling 30 metres (100ft) while walking in the Austrian alps.

Local media reported that the boy was walking with his father when he slipped and fell while crossing rocky terrain in the Tirol mountain range at 11am on Tuesday.

The pair were descending the Gänsekragen mountain after reaching the 2,914m (9,560ft) summit at 9.30am.

They were walking along a waymarked path towards a mountain hut in Winnebachsee when the accident happened about 500m below the summit as the boy rounded a corner.

The 46-year-old man managed to climb down the hillside to his son, who was lying unconscious, and raise the alarm. An air ambulance transported him to a clinic in Innsbruck, where he is being treated for serious injuries.

Police are investigating how the boy fell.

item.title: Schiphol security staff begin strike action over workload
item.description:
Schiphol security staff begin strike action over workload

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Security staff at Schiphol will begin short work stoppages and deliberately slow-downs in the coming days, after the airport and its three security firms missed a union deadline to ease a workload the unions say has become unmanageable. Travellers could face longer queues as a result.

Unions FNV and CNV announced the action on Wednesday, after an ultimatum to Schiphol and the firms Securitas, I-SEC and Trigion expired at midday. The stoppages will be flagged only a few hours in advance, and the unions have not ruled out longer strikes if nothing changes.

“Nobody wants industrial action at Schiphol,” said CNV negotiator André Quist. “But if employers take no concrete step against the enormous workload even after a crystal-clear ultimatum, they leave our members no choice.”

The dispute dates back to a shake-up in the spring, when Schiphol cut the number of firms running hand-baggage checks from five to three. The switch to new employers affected most of the airport’s roughly 5,000 security guards, whose pay was preserved but whose rosters, shift times, breaks and leave all changed.

Since then, the unions say, workloads have risen and sickness absence has climbed, leaving fewer guards to carry the same load – a downward spiral they warn is getting worse.

In July the unions made eight demands, including longer breaks, two consecutive days off after five worked, a heat protocol for the terminals, and at least two women on every security lane so female passengers can be searched. A lane should close, they say, if only one woman is available.

Schiphol said it regretted the action and took the guards’ concerns seriously, adding that it and the three firms were already working on improvements to five of the eight demands. It said it would do all it could to limit the impact on travellers.

A separate walkout by around 350 cleaners at the airport also happened on Wednesday for two hours around midday in a dispute over reduced sick pay in the national cleaning agreement, which FNV wants Schiphol, as a major client, to help resist.

item.title: Dismay for Ajax fans as European tie is screened on PPV channel
item.description:
Dismay for Ajax fans as European tie is screened on PPV channel

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Ajax fans who want to watch the club’s crucial Conference League play-off match against Swiss club Sion will have to pay €4.99 after the broadcasting rights were acquired by Talpa.

The match, which kicks off at 8.15pm on Thursday, is being shown on Talpa’s pay-per-view channel KIJK, angering many Dutch fans.

The decision also went down badly with Ziggo, Ajax’s main sponsor and one of the Netherlands’ biggest commercial sports broadcasters.

Ziggo has the exclusive rights to show matches in UEFA’s main competitions, but qualifying rounds are not covered by that deal.

The company posted a message on social media site X, formerly Twitter, explaining that Sion as the home club was entitled to sell the broadcasting rights to the highest bidder.

Mededeling voor FC Sion – Ajax#ZiggoSport #Ajax #UECL pic.twitter.com/jQBKOncc3P

— Ziggo Sport Voetbal (@ZS_Voetbal) August 17, 2026

The return leg in Amsterdam next Thursday, August 27, will be screen on Ziggo’s free subscription channel.

On Wednesday, NEC Nijmegen will be hoping to take a step towards the Champions League group stages as they host Norwegian side Bodø/Glimt in the first leg of their play-off tie. The match is being shown on Ziggo Sport, with the return leg in Norway next Tuesday, August 25.

item.title: Criminals cashing in on black market for non-deposit cans
item.description:
Criminals cashing in on black market for non-deposit cans

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Criminal gangs are earning millions by importing canned drinks to bypass the Dutch deposit return system.

The black market has sprung up since a compulsory 15 cent deposit was imposed on all drinks cans in 2023, as part of the Dutch government’s plans to cut waste.

The environmental standards inspectorate ILT estimates that up to 50 million illegally imported bottles are sold every year, often in restaurants and cafés that buy them from illegal traders.

In an echo of the Netherlands’ cannabis policy, importing canned drinks is outlawed, but buying and selling them after they cross the border is not, making the drinks attractive to outlets that want to avoid the cost and logistical burden of recycling thousands of cans.

Soft drinks are bought from Germany and Denmark, while beer is more commonly imported from Poland, all countries in the border-free Schengen zone.

The result is that the cans end up in landfill or as litter, hampering the government’s efforts to meet its recycling targets.

“It’s an illegal trade,” ILT acting inspector-general Edwin van Houten told EenVandaag. “They come into contact with organised crime because there is a huge amount of money to be earned from avoiding the rules. It runs into the millions of euros.”

Van Houten said the rules were difficult to enforce because only importation is illegal. In the last year 500 inspections were carried out and 90 companies were given warnings, but only five were fined.

“It’s a drop in the ocean and it costs a lot of capacity because we need to do far-reaching, deep investigations,” he said.

item.title: Parents of euthanasia teen go to court over prosecution letter
item.description:
Parents of euthanasia teen go to court over prosecution letter

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The parents of a 17-year-old girl who chose to die by euthanasia in 2023 due to incurable psychological suffering have gone to court to force public prosecutors to identify a group of doctors that wrote a damning letter about the case.

Their daughter Milou’s psychological struggles were documented in a 2023 documentary, which covered her wish to be granted the right to voluntary death and the aftermath that followed.

The case caused significant public controversy and a group of 14 doctors subsequently wrote a letter suggesting a criminal investigation should be launched against the parents and doctors involved in treating her.

They called on prosecutors to find out “to what extent those close to this vulnerable patient (…) influenced this young patient’s decision to choose euthanasia.” The writers of the letter did not know Milou or her personal background and had not spoken to her themselves.

Eight of the signatories of the letter are still unnamed. In a courtroom in The Hague on Tuesday, the mother of Milou recounted how that letter had led to daily threats and intimidation, requiring the police to guard their home.

“As a parent, losing your child and having to miss them forever is the worst thing that can happen to you,” the mother Mireille Verhoof told the court. “Being accused afterwards of inciting the death of your child or being complicit in her death is beyond description and unbearable.”

She also said her daughter had effectively been “abused” by anti-euthanasia campaigners, who dismissed their integrity to further a political agenda.

The family’s lawyer Richard Korver also said that the people behind the letter should not be able to use their professional authority to make serious accusations and at the same time claim anonymity, reported to Omroep Brabant.

The public prosecution department still does not want to release the names so as to avoid further conflict and ensure people can bring judicial complaints in confidence. It also disputes that the letter was meant as a formal request for criminal proceedings.

The federation of doctors KNMG also condemned the letter, describing it as “indecent and unacceptable.” The court’s decision on the release of the names is expected on September 3.

If you or someone close to you is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. In the Netherlands, call 113 or 0800-0113 (free) for 24/7 support, or visit 113.nl, where the chat service is available in English.

item.title: Dutch shops to stock more GM food after EU relaxes rules in 2028
item.description:
Dutch shops to stock more GM food after EU relaxes rules in 2028

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More genetically modified food is likely to appear in Dutch stores when rules on licensing and labelling are relaxed in two years’ time.

The European parliament passed a law before the summer recess allowing food retailers to stock products containing GM ingredients without labelling them as such, as long as they account for less than 1% of the contents.

The more flexible law was brought in to offset the effect of stricter limits on pesticides, which the EU wanted to halve by 2030, so that growers could use genetic modification to make their crops more resistant to parasites.

But two years ago the EU dropped the pesticides bill, which commission president Ursula von der Leyen said had become “a symbol of polarisation”, while still going ahead with the relaxation of GM rules.

Food products that have been significantly changed by genetic modification will still have to be licensed and labelled under the current rules.

Michelle Habets, a researcher at the Rathenau Institute, a science and technology think tank based in The Hague, said the more flexible rules risked undermining public confidence in supermarkets and other food retailers.

She told NOS she had spoken to dozens of consumers about the new law while it was passing through the European parliament. “Everyone agreed that genetically modified crops should be labelled,” she said.

“People admitted they don’t always study every label in the supermarket, but they think transparency is important, as is the freedom of choice for people who don’t want to eat those crops for whatever reason.”

Jeroen Candel, associate professor of food and agricultural policy at Wageningen University, said GM crops could bring benefits by reducing the need for pesticides, but added a note of caution.

“The new law is based on the idead that we can optimalise the current system of agriculture with new technology,” he said. “But if we do that, we are maintaining a system that is not sustainable in terms of climate and biodiversity.”

item.title: Dutch media attack “chilling” fines for slimming drugs coverage
item.description:
Dutch media attack “chilling” fines for slimming drugs coverage

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch media companies have been hit with fines running into the tens of millions of euros after inspectors ruled that their reporting on weight loss drugs such as Ozempic amounted to advertising.

Editors described the penalties, issued by the health department’s inspectorate IGJ, as “bizarre” and an attack on press freedom.

The verdicts covered newspapers across the range and political spectrum of Dutch media including NRC, the Volkskrant, the Telegraaf and AD.

The inspectors said the coverage of medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro was too positive because it reported that the benefits of the drugs went beyond treating diabetes, the only condition they are prescribed for in the Netherlands.

The Dutch Medicines Act bans advertising for prescription medicines. The IGJ said it had issued around 20 fines between 2023 for breaching the law, not just to media companies.

Science reporting

The inspectorate would not go into individual cases, but DPG Media, one of the two main news publishers in the Netherlands, said it had been fined €48,500 in April for two articles in local newspaper De Stentor and lifestyle magazine Flair, and another €51,000 this month for articles in the Volkskrant and AD.

Mediahuis was fined a total of €132,000 this month for articles in NRC’s science section and the Telegraaf.

The IGJ said: “We weigh up the facts carefully in each case, including the interests of patients. In the case of media coverage we look at the whole picture: content, context, images and audio. It’s not a tick list.”

The journalists’ union NVJ said it was “shocked” that the inspectorate had imposed fines on reporters “who regularly write about medicines and have no other interest than informing the public.”

General secretary Thomas Bruning called for talks with the health ministry to discuss the sanctions. “This makes it impossible for journalists to report on this subject in a normal fashion,” he said. “We are taking it very seriously.”

Press freedom

Pieter Klok, editor of the Volkskrant, said he respected the ban on advertising and the IGJ’s right to enforce it. “But I don’t think it should be applied to journalism, unless you can show it’s been paid for,” he said.

Telegraaf editor Kamran Ullah said it would have a “huge chilling effect” on journalists reporting on health issues.

“That goes not just for large news organisations like us, but maybe even more for smaller titles and freelancers. Big publishers can pay these fines, but a fine of more than €100,000 is the equivalent of two journalists’ annual salary.

“That’s a real infringement of press freedom, because if we have to pay these fines, we can’t employ as many journalists.”

item.title: AI share prices lift household investments to a record high
item.description:
AI share prices lift household investments to a record high

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch households’ investments in the stock market are worth more than ever amid the boom in enthusiasm around AI and technology, the central bank DNB has said.

The total value of shares, funds and bonds held by Dutch households rose about 12% in the second quarter to a record €234.2 billion. It is the sharpest rise in a single quarter since the bank started tracking the figures in 2018.

The gain was almost entirely down to rising share prices, which lifted the value of investments people already owned. Households did not buy more shares – over the quarter they actually sold more than they bought.

ASML, Shell and SpaceX
The fervour around AI adoption has helped ASML, the chip-machine maker, become the most valuable holding in Dutch portfolios, at about €6.1 billion. It pushed Shell, long the most popular investment, into second place at around €4.1 billion, with Rabobank third.

The quarter also saw a massive stock-market debut with Elon Musk’s space company SpaceX listed in New York in June, with Dutch households buying €169 million of its shares in the first month – the most they have ever put into a newly listed company since DNB’s records began.

Many did not hold on for long. A large part was sold again within weeks, probably to lock in the early gains, leaving €71 million still invested by the end of June.

Despite all the gains, investing remains a minority practice in the Netherlands. Only about a quarter of the country’s 8.4 million households invest at all, and the Dutch still keep far more in the bank – around €600 billion in savings – than in the markets.

item.title: Berendsen: Netherlands “disapproves” of new Trump ICC sanctions
item.description:
Berendsen: Netherlands “disapproves” of new Trump ICC sanctions

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch foreign minister Tom Berendsen has criticised the latest sanctions imposed by the Trump administration against officials of the International Criminal Court, based in The Hague.

Berendsen said international courts “must be able to freely carry out their mandates” after the measures were taken against the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and senior prosecutor Abdoulaye Saye.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Akane and Saye had been “directly engaged in efforts by the ICC to investigate, arrest, detain, or prosecute officials whose government ⁠has not consented to ICC jurisdiction.”

Seye was a member of the prosecution team that drafted the arrest warrants against Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s former defence minister Yoav Gallant 18 months ago.

Shortly afterwards Donald Trump issued an executive order authorising sanctions against ICC officials, such as freezing their bank accounts in the US and shutting them out of international payment systems.

The US and Israel are not signatories to the ICC’s founding statutes, but the government of Palestine is. The ICC ruled in 2021 that Gaza and the West Bank fell under its jurisdiction.

Continued support

Berendsen said in a post on social media site X, formerly Twitter: “The Netherlands disapproves of the latest sanctions against officials and staff of the International Criminal Court.”

He went on to offer to meet Akane “to discuss our continued support.” Berendsen did not directly condemn the US government’s actions.

The Netherlands disapproves of the latest sanctions against officials and staff of the International Criminal Court. International courts and tribunals must be able to freely carry out their mandates. 1/2

— Tom Berendsen (@ministerBZ) August 18, 2026


Akane said last year that the sanctions would “rapidly undermine the court’s operations”, while in recent months Rubio has stepped up his rhetoric against the ICC, accusing it of “waging a war against our country” and vowing to dismantle it “brick by brick”.
